title: Every state a guest
hookLine: Rumi teaches that every state of the heart comes to teach and then leaves

lines: A MOOD AT THE KITCHEN TABLE.
SHOVE IT OUT, OR MOVE IT IN?
THE FIFTH BOOK OF THE MASNAVI.
cards: Some mornings you wake up and a mood is already sitting at the kitchen table. Dread about a meeting. A heaviness with no reason.
Sometimes a good one, a lightness you can't explain. With the hard ones, the first instinct is to shove them out the door, or to decide this is who you are now, forever. Rumi had another idea.
You may have seen a poem shared online about the human being as a guest house. That popular English poem is a modern, free version. The older Persian lines are in the fifth book of the Masnavi.

teach.b: Rumi pictures the thoughts and feelings that arrive in you as guests. Each day, at every moment, he says, a new one comes into the heart.
Treat each one with honor, even the sad ones, because a guest comes from somewhere, and each one is sent.
A sorrow may be clearing out the house so a new joy can move in. And guests don't stay. They teach what they came to teach, and they leave.
Sufis had words for this long before Rumi.

teach.h: HAL COMES AND GOES; MAQAM STAYS.
teach.b: A hal is a state: a mood of the heart that comes and goes, like longing, or fear, or joy, or nearness to God. A maqam is a station: something you work for that stays, like patience or trust.
The teachers said you can't hold on to a state, and you shouldn't try. It's a gift, and it moves on.

The Qur'an has a line in the same spirit, revealed after the hard day at Uhud: days like these are passed around among people, turn by turn. Good days and hard days each take their turn, and none moves in for good.
This week had its own guests: Rabi'a and love for its own sake, Junayd and sober love, al-Ghazali, for whom knowing is not tasting, Rumi and the meeting, the reed, the elephant and the candle.
Each came, taught, and moved on to make room for the next.

how: Sufi teachers distinguish passing states, ahwal, from lasting stations, maqamat, and teach students to receive each state with patience and gratitude without clinging to it.

o: a lasting station you work hard to reach
a spiritual retreat for a fixed number of days
a state of the heart that comes and goes

games.q: you wake up and sorrow is already sitting at the kitchen table. what does Rumi say to do?
o: treat it as a guest, with honor, because it was sent.
decide it's who you are now.
games.why: honor the guest, even a sad one: it may be clearing the house for a new joy, and it won't stay.

practice: Notice what's here right now, maybe tiredness, worry, irritation or sadness, and pick one. Instead of pushing it away, open the door to it like a guest: where does it sit in your body, and what might it have come to tell you?
You don't have to agree with it; just treat it with courtesy, remember it's not moving in, and if you pray, ask God what the guest was sent to teach.

wordCard.voice: Hal. A state of the heart that comes and goes — Rumi's picture of every mood as a guest that teaches, then leaves. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a state of the heart that comes and goes; plural ahwal. contrasted with maqam, a lasting station.

carryVoice: Your line: every state is a guest. Even the sad ones come from somewhere. Day three hundred one, and the week is done.
